supervisorWelcome: Welcome to the laboratory! Before beginning your research, you need to complete a safety inspection. Some things in this lab are unsafe. Can you find them and decide how to fix them?

hazards.title: Blocked emergency exit
hazards.explanation: Emergency exits must be 100% clear at all times. Move the cart to a designated storage area, not just aside.
hazards.criticalReason: an emergency exit must never be blocked or left partly obstructed, even for a short time.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: an emergency exit must be completely clear at all times.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice that the emergency exit was blocked by a cart.

questions.question: What should you do about the cart blocking the emergency exit?
questions.explanation: In an evacuation many people rush out at once, maybe in smoke. A half-blocked exit or a sign on the cart doesn't help them, so the cart has to go.

options.text: Move the cart enough for one person to pass.
Move the cart to storage, leaving the exit completely clear.
Leave the cart until the next scheduled supply delivery.
Put a warning sign on the cart to alert others.

questions.question: How can you confirm the emergency exit is safe to use?
questions.explanation: An exit is only usable if the whole path to safety is clear, not just the door itself.

options.text: The green emergency exit sign is clearly visible.
The cart no longer touches the emergency door.
One person can pass through the door sideways.
The door and entire escape route are unobstructed.

questions.question: The team needs the cart again in ten minutes. What should you do?
questions.explanation: An emergency can happen in those ten minutes too, so the cart never waits in front of the exit.

options.text: Park it in a designated area away from the exit.
Keep it near the exit with some walking space.
Leave it there and set a reminder to move it later.
Move it in front of a different emergency door.

hazards.title: Food and drink on the bench
hazards.explanation: Food and drink are strictly prohibited in the laboratory because of ingestion and contamination risk.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: food and drink are never allowed in the lab.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice food and drink on the lab bench.

questions.question: You notice a coffee cup beside active lab equipment. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Drinks near lab equipment can pick up chemical residue and be swallowed. Drink only outside the lab.

options.text: Move the cup to the far side of the bench.
Close the lid and continue the experiment as planned.
Take the drink to an approved area outside the laboratory.
Place the cup inside a drawer until work finishes.

questions.question: A colleague wants coffee during a long experiment. What should you suggest?
questions.explanation: A spill-proof cup or a closed lid is still a drink in the lab. A short break outside the lab is the safe way to drink.

options.text: Take a break and drink in an approved non-lab area.
Use a spill-proof cup at the edge of the bench.
Have someone hold the cup away from the samples.
Keep the beverage closed until the experiment finishes.

questions.question: Why is a closed coffee cup still a safety concern in the laboratory?
questions.explanation: The lid keeps the coffee in, not the chemicals out. Residue on your gloves, hands and the outside of the cup reaches your mouth with the next sip.

options.text: It could tip over and spill onto the experiment.
The container could reduce available working space.
The heat from the coffee could affect nearby samples.
Residue from your hands and the cup ends up in your mouth.

hazards.title: Unstably stacked boxes
hazards.explanation: Unstable stacks can fall on people. Unstack them and store items safely at a lower height.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: unstable stacks must be taken down and stored low.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice the unstable stack of boxes near the walkway.

questions.question: Several cardboard boxes are leaning dangerously. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Taping or straightening the stack still leaves heavy boxes at height. Lower, stable storage removes the fall hazard.

options.text: Unstack the boxes and move them to stable, lower storage.
Secure the boxes together using tape and plastic wrap.
Align the upper boxes and leave them on the crate.
Move the crate closer to the wall beside the walkway.

questions.question: What is the main danger of the unstable boxes?
questions.explanation: A falling stack can injure people in the walkway and block it.

options.text: The boxes could get crushed and damage what's inside.
The crate may occupy too much storage space.
The boxes could fall onto people using the walkway.
The cardboard may be difficult to clean properly.

questions.question: How should deliveries be stored to prevent this problem?
questions.explanation: Heavy boxes at the bottom and low stacks can't topple onto anyone. Tape or wrap only holds a bad stack together until it falls.

options.text: Put lighter boxes on top without checking stability.
Put them on shelves: heavy boxes low, nothing stacked above shoulder height.
Keep all deliveries on crates beside active walkways.
Wrap boxes tightly even when they extend beyond the crate.

hazards.title: Lab coat on a chair
hazards.explanation: Lab coats can carry contamination. Store them on a designated hook or rack away from seating and work areas.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: a used lab coat goes on its hook, or in a sealed bag if contaminated.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice the lab coat left on a chair.

questions.question: Where should the lab coat be stored after use?
questions.explanation: A used coat can carry chemical residue. On its hook it doesn't touch seats, bags or your own clothes.

options.text: Fold the coat and place it on the lab bench.
Leave the coat on the chair until the next experiment.
Put it in your locker with your bag and jacket.
Hang it on the lab coat hook, away from seats and bags.

questions.question: What should you do if the lab coat may be contaminated?
questions.explanation: A contaminated coat comes off right away and is cleaned by the lab. Shaking it out, wearing it again or washing it at home spreads the chemical.

options.text: Shake off any residue and hang it to dry.
Take it off, seal it in a bag and tell your supervisor.
Take it home and wash it with your normal laundry.
Wear the coat again after checking for visible stains.

questions.question: Why should lab coats not be left on shared chairs?
questions.explanation: Anyone can sit there next, in normal clothes. Residue on the coat rubs off onto the chair and then onto them.

options.text: They make chairs harder to move around the bench.
They reduce the number of seats available to colleagues.
Residue can rub off onto the chair and the next person.
They make the laboratory appear less organized.

hazards.title: Improper waste separation
hazards.explanation: Lab waste must be separated from domestic waste and go into the designated lab waste container.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: anything used in lab work goes in lab waste, not the normal bin.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice used gloves in the general waste bin.

questions.question: Used lab gloves are in the domestic waste bin. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Lab gloves may carry chemical residue. In the normal bin they reach cleaners and household trash, where nobody expects chemicals.

options.text: Cover the used gloves with more regular office waste.
Move them into the marked lab waste bin.
Move the gloves into the recycling bin for plastics.
Leave the gloves there until the next waste collection.

questions.question: You are unsure whether an item requires special waste handling. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Guessing can put hazardous waste in the wrong bin. The waste sign or your supervisor tells you where it goes.

options.text: Treat the item as regular waste if it appears dry.
Ask cleaning staff to select the bin during collection.
Choose the nearest available bin to avoid further handling.
Check the waste sign at the bins or ask your supervisor.

questions.question: Which item can normally go into domestic waste?
questions.explanation: Only items that never entered lab work, like a clean wrapper from the break room, count as domestic waste.

options.text: A clean snack wrapper from the designated break room.
A used pipette tip from an active laboratory bench.
Gloves removed after handling unknown laboratory chemicals.
An unidentified liquid from a reagent storage bottle.

hazards.title: Unlabeled chemical bottle
hazards.explanation: Never smell or pour away an unknown chemical. Isolate it and let the supervisor/HSE identify, label or dispose of it.
hazards.criticalReason: unknown chemicals must never be identified by smell or poured into the drain; they must be isolated and identified by HSE.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: never smell, pour away or reuse an unknown chemical.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice the unlabeled chemical bottle.

questions.question: You find a bottle containing an unknown clear liquid. What should you do?
questions.explanation: An unknown liquid could be anything. Keep it closed and out of use so no one smells, uses or pours it away.

options.text: Open the bottle and compare its smell with known reagents.
Test a small sample using indicator paper without reporting it.
Keep it closed, prevent its use, and notify the supervisor.
Add a temporary label based on its storage location.

questions.question: A colleague says the liquid must be water because it is clear. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Acids, bleach and many solvents look just like water, and pouring some down the sink can react or give off fumes. Looking at it tells you nothing.

options.text: Pour a small amount into the sink to check it.
Don't use it; set it aside until the supervisor identifies it.
Use the liquid only for simple cleaning tasks.
Compare its appearance against other transparent liquids.

questions.question: What must happen before this bottle returns to normal chemical storage?
questions.explanation: Everyone relies on the label to know what's in a bottle. Until it is identified and labelled, the next person faces the same unknown.

options.text: The bottle is placed in secondary containment overnight.
A colleague confirms that the liquid appears harmless.
A temporary note identifies the contents as unknown.
It is identified and gets a full label: name, hazards and date.

hazards.title: Missing PPE and headphones
hazards.explanation: Wear the required safety glasses and remove headphones so you can hear alarms and colleagues.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: wear safety glasses and keep your ears free for alarms.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice the unused safety glasses and headphones at the bench.

questions.question: You see safety glasses and headphones beside an active workstation. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Safety eyewear protects against splashes, and without headphones you can hear alarms and colleagues.

options.text: Wear the required safety eyewear and remove the headphones.
Keep the headphones but wear regular glasses during work.
Wear safety goggles only when handling visible chemicals.
Lower the headphone volume and leave the goggles nearby.

questions.question: You already wear prescription glasses. What is the appropriate eye protection?
questions.explanation: Normal glasses aren't made to stop splashes or flying glass, and leave gaps at the sides. Goggles fit over them.

options.text: Wear ordinary glasses if their lenses are sufficiently thick.
Use a face shield instead of wearing safety glasses.
Wear safety goggles over your glasses, or prescription safety glasses.
Work farther from the bench to avoid eye exposure.

questions.question: Why should headphones be removed during active laboratory work?
questions.explanation: Headphones can mask fire alarms and warnings shouted by colleagues.

options.text: They are only a problem when the music is loud.
They may prevent you from hearing alarms or colleagues.
They can cause interference with nearby laboratory computers.
Headphones may become uncomfortable during long experiments.

hazards.title: Damaged power cable
hazards.explanation: Damaged cables are a shock and fire risk. Unplug and tag the equipment out of service and report it for replacement.
hazards.criticalReason: continuing to use, taping or hiding a damaged cable keeps a live shock and fire hazard in service.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: damaged cables and overloaded adapters must be unplugged and fixed.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not detect the damaged cable and overloaded power strip.

questions.question: You discover a power cable with exposed wires. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Exposed wires can shock you or start a fire. Unplugged and tagged, nobody can use it by mistake before it is fixed.

options.text: Cover the damaged wires with tape before using the device.
Push the damaged cable behind the equipment until inspection.
Keep using it, but don't touch the damaged part.
Switch it off, unplug it, tag it 'Do not use' and report it.

questions.question: Several high-power devices are connected to one adapter. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Too many high-power devices on one adapter overheat it and can start a fire. Separate wall sockets share the load; another adapter just moves the problem.

options.text: Spread them over separate wall sockets; report it if there aren't enough.
Add another adapter to distribute the cables across sockets.
Switch on devices one at a time to prevent overheating.
Move the adapter beneath the workbench to avoid contact.

questions.criticalReason: overloading an adapter with high-power devices can overheat it and start a fire.

questions.question: When can equipment with a previously damaged cable be used again?
questions.explanation: Tape or a test run that works doesn't fix a damaged cable. Only a proper repair and check make it safe again.

options.text: After the frayed cable is covered with insulating material.
After the device demonstrates stable power during startup.
After an electrician repairs it and checks that it is safe.
After a colleague completes one successful test run.

hazards.title: Blocked / incomplete first-aid kit
hazards.explanation: Emergency equipment must be accessible and complete. Clear access and report the missing supplies to HSE.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: first-aid kits must be accessible and fully stocked.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not detect that the cabinet was blocked and supplies were missing.

questions.question: Bottles are blocking access to the first-aid cabinet. What should you do?
questions.explanation: In an emergency every second counts, so the first-aid cabinet must be reachable immediately.

options.text: Place an additional sign near the cabinet and leave the bottles.
Remove the obstructions so the cabinet is immediately accessible.
Use another first-aid kit without reporting the blocked cabinet.
Close the cabinet and ask colleagues to avoid the area.

questions.question: You notice that several essential first-aid supplies are missing. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Report missing supplies so they are restocked before someone needs them.

options.text: Rearrange the remaining supplies to cover the empty spaces.
Ask colleagues to bring personal supplies until the next inspection.
Wait until someone needs those supplies before requesting replacements.
Tell whoever looks after the kit what's missing so it gets restocked.

questions.question: What should be checked during a routine first-aid inspection?
questions.explanation: A kit that is blocked, half empty or out of date lets you down exactly when someone is hurt.

options.text: It is easy to reach, nothing is missing and nothing has expired.
The cabinet has no visible scratches, fingerprints, or other marks.
Every item is stored above eye level to prevent misuse.
The cabinet is locked to prevent unnecessary access.

hazards.title: Improper chemical storage
hazards.explanation: Corrosives belong low down in secondary containment, separated from incompatible substances such as flammables.
hazards.criticalReason: corrosives must not be stored high up or with incompatible substances; a fall or reaction can cause severe injury.
hazards.wrongFeedback: Not safe: corrosives go low, in secondary containment, away from flammables.
hazards.missedFeedback: The student did not notice corrosive acid stored high up next to flammables.

questions.question: A corrosive acid bottle is stored on a high shelf. Where should it be kept?
questions.explanation: Low down it can't fall on anyone, and the spill tray catches any leak.

options.text: On the upper shelf with a larger hazard warning label.
On the same shelf, grouped with similar-sized chemical bottles.
Low down in the acid cabinet, standing in a spill tray.
In the laboratory refrigerator to reduce possible vapor release.

questions.question: How should corrosive acids and incompatible chemicals be organized?
questions.explanation: If incompatible chemicals leak into each other they can get hot, give off fumes or catch fire. Sort by what reacts with what, not by size or colour.

options.text: Keep acids away from flammables and anything else they react with.
Group substances according to bottle size and label color.
Place all liquid chemicals in the same containment tray.
Store corrosive and flammable chemicals together to save space.

questions.question: Why is storing HCl above head height beside incompatible chemicals dangerous?
questions.explanation: A bottle falling from above head height can splash acid onto the face and eyes, and react with what it lands on.

options.text: Smaller chemical bottles may become difficult to locate.
If it falls, acid can splash your face and react with other bottles.
Chemical labels may fade more quickly on upper shelves.
The arrangement may appear disorganized during safety inspections.
